title: Git Internals: DAG
description: Commit history as a Directed Acyclic Graph

content.overview: In this module, you'll learn how Git uses a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) to represent the commit history of a repository. Understanding this data structure is essential for mastering Git's branching, merging, and history manipulation capabilities.

steps.title: Introduction to DAGs in Git
steps.content: A Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) is a graph that has directed edges and no cycles. In Git, each commit is a node in the graph, and each commit points to its parent commit(s), forming a directed graph. Since a commit cannot be its own ancestor (which would create a cycle), Git's commit history forms a DAG.

steps.title: Creating a Simple Commit History
steps.content: Let's create a new repository and make a few commits to see how Git builds a DAG of commits.

commands.description: Create a directory for our demo

commands.expectedOutput: Initialized empty Git repository in dag-demo/.git/

commands.description: Add the file to the staging area

commands.expectedOutput:
[master (root-commit) xxxxxxx] Commit A: Initial commit
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 file.txt

behindTheCommand.title: Anatomy of the First Commit
behindTheCommand.content:
When you make the first commit in a repository:

1. Git creates a commit object with metadata (author, timestamp, message)
2. The commit points to a tree object representing the project's file structure
3. Since it's the first commit, it has no parent commits
4. Git updates the HEAD reference and the master branch to point to this commit

This first commit becomes the root node of the DAG that will grow as you add more commits.

steps.title: Adding More Commits
steps.content: Let's add more commits to our repository to see how the DAG grows.

commands.command: git commit -m "Commit B: Add second line"
commands.expectedOutput:
[master xxxxxxx] Commit B: Add second line
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)

commands.command: git commit -m "Commit C: Add third line"
commands.expectedOutput:
[master xxxxxxx] Commit C: Add third line
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)

behindTheCommand.title: Building the Commit Graph
behindTheCommand.content:
As you add more commits to the repository:

1. Each new commit points to its parent commit (the previous HEAD)
2. This creates a chain of commits, forming a linear path in the DAG
3. The branch reference (master) and HEAD move forward to point to the newest commit
4. Each commit represents a snapshot of the entire repository at that point in time

This linear chain is the simplest form of a DAG, but Git's DAG becomes more interesting when we introduce branching and merging.

steps.title: Visualizing the Commit Graph
steps.content: Git provides several commands to visualize the commit graph, which helps you understand the structure of the DAG.

commands.expectedOutput:
xxxxxxx (HEAD -> master) Commit C: Add third line
xxxxxxx Commit B: Add second line
xxxxxxx Commit A: Initial commit

commands.description: View the commit history as a graph
commands.expectedOutput:
* xxxxxxx (HEAD -> master) Commit C: Add third line
* xxxxxxx Commit B: Add second line
* xxxxxxx Commit A: Initial commit

behindTheCommand.title: Traversing the DAG for Log Output
behindTheCommand.content:
When you run `git log`, Git traverses the commit DAG starting from HEAD:

1. It visits the commit that HEAD points to
2. Then it follows the parent pointer to the previous commit
3. It continues following parent pointers until it reaches a commit with no parents (the root commit)
4. For each commit visited, it displays the commit information

The `--graph` option visualizes the DAG structure, showing branches and merges with ASCII art. For a linear history like ours so far, this doesn't show much, but it becomes very useful when the history includes branches and merges.

steps.title: Creating Branches
steps.content: Branches in Git are simply pointers to specific commits in the DAG. Creating a branch adds a new reference but doesn't change the DAG structure itself.

commands.description: View the commit graph with all branches
commands.expectedOutput:
* xxxxxxx (HEAD -> master, feature) Commit C: Add third line
* xxxxxxx Commit B: Add second line
* xxxxxxx Commit A: Initial commit

behindTheCommand.title: Branches as References to Commits
behindTheCommand.content:
When you create a branch in Git:

1. Git adds a new reference (pointer) to the current commit
2. This reference is stored in `.git/refs/heads/[branch-name]`
3. The DAG structure itself doesn't change
4. Both branches point to the same commit until you make new commits on either branch

Branches are lightweight in Git because they're just references to commits in the DAG, not separate copies of the code.

steps.title: Diverging History with Branches
steps.content: Let's switch to the feature branch and make some commits to see how the DAG structure diverges.

commands.description: Create a new file in the feature branch

commands.command: git commit -m "Commit D: Add feature file"
commands.expectedOutput:
[feature xxxxxxx] Commit D: Add feature file
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 feature.txt

commands.description: Switch back to the master branch
Create a new file in the master branch

commands.command: git commit -m "Commit E: Add master file"
commands.expectedOutput:
[master xxxxxxx] Commit E: Add master file
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 master.txt

behindTheCommand.title: Branching in the DAG
behindTheCommand.content:
When you make commits on different branches:

1. The DAG structure diverges, with each branch forming its own path
2. Both paths share a common history (the commits before the branch point)
3. Each branch reference moves forward independently with new commits
4. HEAD points to the current branch, which points to the latest commit on that branch

This divergence in the DAG is what allows Git to maintain multiple lines of development simultaneously.

steps.title: Visualizing the Diverged Graph
steps.content: Now that our history has diverged, let's visualize the DAG to see the branch structure.

commands.description: View the commit graph with all branches
commands.expectedOutput:
* xxxxxxx (HEAD -> master) Commit E: Add master file
| * xxxxxxx (feature) Commit D: Add feature file
|/
* xxxxxxx Commit C: Add third line
* xxxxxxx Commit B: Add second line
* xxxxxxx Commit A: Initial commit

behindTheCommand.title: Visualizing Divergent Paths in the DAG
behindTheCommand.content:
The `git log --graph` output shows the structure of the DAG:

1. The asterisks (*) represent commits
2. The lines and slashes (|/) show the connections between commits
3. Branch names appear next to the commits they point to
4. HEAD indicates the current branch

This visualization helps you understand the branching structure and how commits relate to each other in the DAG.

steps.title: Merging Branches
steps.content: Merging branches creates a new commit with multiple parents, which is where the DAG structure becomes more complex and interesting.

commands.command: git merge feature -m "Commit F: Merge feature into master"
commands.description: Merge the feature branch into master
commands.expectedOutput:
Merge made by the 'recursive' strategy.
 feature.txt | 1 +
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 feature.txt

commands.description: View the commit graph after the merge
commands.expectedOutput:
*   xxxxxxx (HEAD -> master) Commit F: Merge feature into master
|\  
| * xxxxxxx (feature) Commit D: Add feature file
* | xxxxxxx Commit E: Add master file
|/  
* xxxxxxx Commit C: Add third line
* xxxxxxx Commit B: Add second line
* xxxxxxx Commit A: Initial commit

behindTheCommand.title: Merge Commits in the DAG
behindTheCommand.content:
When you merge branches in Git:

1. Git creates a new commit (the merge commit) with two parent commits
2. The first parent is the commit that the current branch pointed to
3. The second parent is the commit that the merged branch pointed to
4. This creates a diamond shape in the DAG, joining the divergent paths
5. The current branch reference moves to the new merge commit

Merge commits are special because they have multiple parents, which is what makes Git's history a DAG rather than just a tree or a linear list.

steps.title: Examining Merge Commit Structure
steps.content: Let's examine the structure of the merge commit to see how it references multiple parents.

commands.expectedOutput:
tree xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
parent xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
parent xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
author Your Name <your.email@example.com> timestamp
committer Your Name <your.email@example.com> timestamp

Commit F: Merge feature into master

commit xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
tree xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
parent xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
parent xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
author Your Name <your.email@example.com> timestamp
committer Your Name <your.email@example.com> timestamp

    Commit F: Merge feature into master

behindTheCommand.title: Anatomy of a Merge Commit
behindTheCommand.content:
A merge commit differs from a regular commit in its internal structure:

1. Regular commits have a single parent reference
2. Merge commits have multiple parent references (typically two)
3. The first parent is the commit on the current branch before the merge
4. The second parent is the tip of the branch being merged in
5. Git uses this parent information to traverse the DAG correctly

This multi-parent structure is what allows Git to represent complex branching and merging patterns in its history.
